prompt: Introduce yourself to the panel.
guidance: Keep it under a minute: name, where you trained, who you work/worked under, the one project in your portfolio, and a one-line summary of your role on it. Stay formal and confident.
sampleAnswer: Good morning/evening sir/ma, my name is [your name]. I trained as an architect and worked under the supervision of Arc. Ramota Obagah-Stephen of Crinck Associates Ltd, where I was involved in the design and construction of a four-bedroom residential duplex in Rumuokparali Town, Rivers State, from inception through to handover.

prompt: A panel member criticises your drawings or brief sharply (e.g. 'your drawings look underdeveloped, you should have added more landscaping/facade detail'). How do you respond?
guidance: Do not get defensive or over-apologise repeatedly. A short, composed acknowledgement is enough, then pivot back to substance if you get the chance. From the real Team 6 transcript: the candidate simply said 'Thank you sir, I'm sorry sir' and moved on calmly — brevity and composure read better than over-explaining or arguing.
sampleAnswer: Thank you for the observation, sir. Noted — landscaping and facade articulation were areas I would develop further given more scope on this project.

prompt: Tell us how you participated in the project.
guidance: Walk through your actual stage-by-stage role, not a generic description. Be ready to be specific and ready to be interrupted with follow-ups on any stage you mention.
sampleAnswer: I attended the brief-taking with my supervisor, prepared the hand-drawn concept bubble diagrams, produced the architectural working drawings, checked consultants' drawings for clashes, personally inspected the suspended floor slab before casting, carried out regular site visits, and took part in snagging and close-out.

prompt: What type of contract was used on your project, and how were the contractors paid?
guidance: Know your actual contract type cold (priced bill of quantities), and be ready to explain the payment mechanism in your own words — interim valuations by the quantity surveyor, paid as work is certified complete.
sampleAnswer: It was a building contract based on a priced bill of quantities. The quantity surveyor valued completed work, and the contractor was paid against those valuations as the works progressed in stages, since the clients were funding the project as money became available.

prompt: (Alternative project type) If your contract were Design-and-Build, how would payment typically be structured?
guidance: This is from a real transcript example — know the general pattern even if it wasn't your own contract type, since panels ask about contract types generally, not just the one in your portfolio. Design-and-Build payments are commonly tied to milestone completion rather than interim bill-of-quantities valuations.
sampleAnswer: In a Design-and-Build arrangement, the contractor takes on both design and construction responsibility, and payment is typically made on completion of agreed milestones rather than itemised BoQ valuations.

prompt: What alterations were made during the project, and how were they handled?
guidance: Have one concrete example ready (design or site-driven), and describe the process: who raised it, who approved it, how it was recorded.
sampleAnswer: Minor layout adjustments were needed during design development to align the structural columns between floors, which meant revising some room sizes. These were coordinated with the structural engineer, reviewed by my supervisor, and the revised drawings were reissued to all consultants.

prompt: Why did construction take as long as it did?
guidance: Be honest and specific, don't deflect. Funding-phased construction and weather are both legitimate, common, defensible reasons — own them rather than being vague.
sampleAnswer: Two main factors: the clients funded the works in phases as money became available rather than all at once, and the rainy season affected progress during site works. Construction ran about 200 days in total, with planned pauses between funded phases.

prompt: Did you have site meetings, and what was your role in them?
guidance: Describe the actual mechanics: who attended, how often, what you personally reported.
sampleAnswer: Yes, site meetings were held with the contractor, the project manager and consultants when needed. My role was to visit the site regularly, observe progress and quality, and report my findings to my supervisor, who then gave instructions to the contractor.

prompt: A panel member asks a pointed, specific technical question about an unusual part of your brief — e.g. 'what does your client want to do with the space behind the building', or a structural dimension on a specific design element.
guidance: This tests whether you actually know your own drawings in detail, not just the narrative. Review your site plan, sections and any unusual spatial features tonight so you're not caught flat-footed on something visible in your own drawings.
sampleAnswer: N/A — prepare your own project's specifics here. For Blueprint Drills' project: the area behind the building is unbuilt plot (334.094 sqm of the 464.301 sqm plot is unbuilt — about 72% — be ready to say what it's used for, e.g. future expansion, garden, parking).

prompt: (Example from a transcript, different project) 'You designed a supermarket with large halls — what were the column sizes and spacing?'
guidance: This illustrates the kind of structural-sizing question examiners ask about any large-span space in your portfolio. If your own project has any large clear-span room, know its structural grid, column size and spacing before you go in.
sampleAnswer: N/A — be ready with real numbers from your own drawings for any large-span space you designed.

prompt: If you become an architect today, what would you advocate for from the NIA and ARCON concerning architects?
guidance: Have a genuine, considered position ready — this is explicitly listed as something panels probe. A real, specific example (not a generic platitude) lands better. One strong real example: advocating for better treatment and site provisions (e.g. conveniences/facilities) for female architects.
sampleAnswer: I would advocate for better treatment of female architects and provisions for them on site — basic things like adequate conveniences — since site environments are not always designed with that in mind.

prompt: Follow-up: a panel member asks if a claim you made (e.g. about site treatment of a group) is really true, or challenges you to justify it.
guidance: If you have a real, specific personal example, use it — it's far stronger than a general claim. From the real transcript: a candidate was challenged on whether unequal site treatment of female architects 'makes sense,' and responded with a personal account of having been confronted by site workers, which the panel accepted. Don't fabricate an example if you don't have one — pivot to a credible general industry observation instead.
sampleAnswer: Yes — I experienced this directly myself on a site visit, which is part of why I raised it.

prompt: What do you do for leisure?
guidance: A simple, genuine answer is fine — this is a rapport/personality check, not a trick question. Keep it brief.
sampleAnswer: I enjoy swimming and playing video games with my family.

prompt: What is happening in Nigeria currently?
guidance: Have 1-2 genuine, current, non-controversial current-events items ready the night before (check the news that morning) — political, economic or infrastructure news is safest. Avoid sounding uninformed or giving a stale answer.
sampleAnswer: Update this the morning of your interview with 1-2 real current headlines — political and economic developments are the safest ground.

prompt: How is Nigeria's current economic situation affecting architectural practice?
guidance: This is explicitly listed in the official orals guidance as a probed topic. Have a real, considered view: material cost inflation, clients funding projects in phases (you have a real example of this from your own project), naira volatility affecting imported materials, etc.
sampleAnswer: Rising material costs and naira volatility mean many clients now fund projects in phases rather than all at once — I experienced this directly on my own portfolio project, where construction had to proceed as the clients' funds became available.

prompt: What is ARCON and what does it do?
guidance: Know this cold: Architects Registration Council of Nigeria, the statutory body regulating architectural practice and protecting the title 'Architect', founded 1969.
sampleAnswer: ARCON is the Architects Registration Council of Nigeria, the statutory regulatory body that registers architects, regulates practice, and protects the professional title 'Architect'. It was established in 1969.

prompt: What's the difference between NIA and ARCON?
guidance: NIA (Nigerian Institute of Architects) is the professional membership association; ARCON is the statutory regulator with legal registration power. Don't conflate them.
sampleAnswer: NIA is the professional association architects belong to for advocacy, networking and professional development, while ARCON is the statutory body that legally registers and regulates architects and enforces the Architects (Registration, etc.) Act.

prompt: What happens if someone practices architecture without being registered with ARCON?
guidance: Know the consequences: fines, imprisonment, disqualification from government contracts, and the title 'Architect' being legally protected.
sampleAnswer: Practicing or holding yourself out as an architect without ARCON registration is an offence — it can lead to fines, imprisonment, and disqualification from government contracts, since the title is legally protected.

prompt: What is an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) and when is it required?
guidance: Be ready for a scenario follow-up: what would you do if an EIA came back negative on a project you were working on?
sampleAnswer: An EIA assesses the likely environmental effects of a proposed development before it proceeds, and is required for projects with significant potential environmental impact. If an EIA raised serious concerns, I would weigh the risks against the benefits, and not proceed if the risks outweighed the benefits to the environment and community.

prompt: What building contract forms are you aware of, and what is JCT?
guidance: JCT (Joint Contracts Tribunal) publishes standard forms of building contract widely referenced in Commonwealth/Nigerian practice. Know that different JCT forms suit different project types (e.g. traditional/lump sum, design-and-build), and be ready to contrast with FIDIC forms used on larger/international projects.
sampleAnswer: JCT, the Joint Contracts Tribunal, publishes standard forms of building contract — different forms exist for traditional lump-sum contracts, design-and-build, and other arrangements, setting out standard obligations, payment and dispute-resolution mechanisms between employer and contractor.

prompt: What is the Nigerian National Building Code and why does it matter?
guidance: Know its purpose: minimum standards for safety, structural integrity and habitability in building design and construction in Nigeria, and that compliance is tied to the approval process your drawings went through.
sampleAnswer: The National Building Code sets minimum standards for the design, construction and safety of buildings in Nigeria. It matters because compliance is required for planning approval — my own working drawings were submitted to and approved by the planning authority before construction began.
